 "id": "Q08",
 "sourceFile": "The implementation of velocity-based training paradigm for team sports - Framework, technologies, practical recommendations and challenges.pdf",
 "decision": "INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason": "",
 "degradedReason": "",
 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "Text title 'The Implementation of Velocity-Based Training Paradigm for Team Sports: Framework, Technologies, Practical Recommendations and Challenges' matches the filename.",
 "confidence": "high",
 "studyDesign": "Narrative Review",
 "primaryDomain": "Training & Performance",
 "domains": ["Training & Performance", "Monitoring & Technology"],
 "audiences": ["Performance", "Athletic Training", "Coaching"],
 "sports": ["Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations": ["Mixed / Unspecified"],
 "evidenceSummary": "Narrative review and practical framework for velocity-based training (VBT) in team sports. It covers the limits of 1RM testing, the validity and error sources of velocity-tracking devices, individual load-velocity profiling with 4 to 6 incremental loads, combining velocity with repetitions in reserve, and monitoring trends over time. It includes worked examples (an 8-week load table and one player's profile) and presents no new study data; the text describes no search method.",
 "screeningLimitations": "No search strategy or appraisal of the studies cited is described, and most recommendations rest on the authors' experience and on barbell lifts in controlled settings. The worked examples come from single individuals, and the abstract names injury prevention as an aim without evidence for it in the text.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could treat the proposed load-velocity profiling and velocity-loss cut-offs as validated for all team-sport athletes and exercises, when the paper is an expert framework built on barbell lifts and individual examples and it states that velocity relationships differ by exercise, sex, age and training status.",
 "paper": {
   "year": 2021,
   "citation": "Balsalobre-Fernández C, Torres-Ronda L. The Implementation of Velocity-Based Training Paradigm for Team Sports: Framework, Technologies, Practical Recommendations and Challenges. Sports. 2021;9:47.",
   "doi": "10.3390/sports9040047",
   "abstract": "A review of velocity-based training (VBT) for resistance training in team sports. It covers the limits of 1RM-based prescription, velocity-tracking technologies, individual load-velocity profiling, combining velocity with repetitions in reserve, velocity-loss thresholds, and monitoring of individual performance trends. The authors present practical recommendations and discuss the limits of 'muscle power' measurement from velocity devices.",
   "tldr": "Velocity-based training uses bar speed to set and check loads, so training can match each athlete's daily capacity. In team sports, this is best done with individual load-velocity profiles, validated devices, and repetitions in reserve.",
   "methods": "Narrative review and practical framework. The paper describes no search strategy. It uses worked examples, a load-velocity profiling protocol with 4 to 6 incremental loads, and an illustrative 8-week load table, with no new data collected.",
   "findings": "The authors argue that 1RM-based loads can be inaccurate on a given day, and that load-velocity relationships differ by exercise, athlete and training status. Velocity-tracking devices differ in validity and reliability, and 'power' calculated from velocity alone can misrepresent the true output. Velocity loss of about 10 to 20 percent is cited as giving similar physical gains to larger losses with less volume, and a profile R2 below 0.92 is suggested as a prompt to repeat the test.",
   "limitations": "The paper does not describe how sources were selected or appraised, and it presents no new data. Recommendations are largely expert-based, the examples are individual cases, and the velocity-loss and profile thresholds are the authors' experience as well as cited work. Injury prevention is named as an aim without supporting evidence in the text.",
   "practicalImplications": "Coaches of large team-sport squads can measure bar velocity in a warm-up set and adjust loads that day, rebuild load-velocity profiles every 4 to 6 weeks, and use repetitions in reserve for exercises without velocity measurement. Device choice should stay consistent, and 'muscle power' from a velocity device should not be treated as a measure of true power.",
   "athleteDev": "Developing team-sport athletes can be trained with individual load-velocity profiles and velocity thresholds that track their progress. The paper suggests that load-velocity profiles change with training, so profiles should be rechecked as athletes develop.",
   "rtp": "The paper names return to play only briefly and offers no return-to-play protocol. It cannot show when an injured athlete is ready to load, although velocity monitoring could be used as one part of a return-to-training plan."
 }
}

Device choice should stay consistent, and 'muscle power' from a velocity device should not be treated as a measure of true power.",

15	                                          monitoring resistance training programs, its implementation remains a challenge in team sports,
16	                                          where there are still some confusion and misinterpretations of its applications. In addition, in contexts
17	                                          with large squads, it is paramount to understand how to best use movement velocity in different
18	                                          exercises in a useful and time-efficient way. This manuscript aims to provide clarifications on the
19	                                          velocity-based training paradigm, movement velocity tracking technologies, assessment procedures
20	                                          and practical recommendations for its application during resistance training sessions, with the
21	                                          purpose of increasing performance, managing fatigue and preventing injuries. Guidelines to combine
22	                                          velocity metrics with subjective scales to prescribe training loads are presented, as well as methods

35	Academic Editor: Corrado Lupo
36	                                                The importance of resistance training (RT) in team sports, either due to the extensive
37	                                          scientific (and empirical) justification, or its impact in improving overall performance [1,2],
38	Received: 8 March 2021

51	                                          obtain objective information to analyze whether they are achieving the desired results with
52	                                          their program, how the improvements (or setbacks) occur, and thus, can improve their

56	                                                Two of the most frequent indicators used as a reference to prescribe RT have been

58	                                          the 1-Repetition Maximum (1RM) and the maximum number of repetitions at a given
59	distributed under the terms and           percentage of this weight (n1RM%) [5,6]. However, despite being useful to some extent

62	creativecommons.org/licenses/by/          of strength training programs. A still emerging method, although not new, is the velocity-
63	4.0/).                                    based training (VBT), representing both a less invasive and a more optimal method to

67	Sports 2021, 9, 47. https://doi.org/10.3390/sports9040047                                                       https://www.mdpi.com/journal/sports

70

72	                     prescribe RT based on velocity of execution. This is a key element in most sport disciplines,
73	                     either by the requirements of the sport (e.g., sprinting, accelerating/decelerating, jumping,
74	                     throwing, kicking) or as an indicator of intensity (e.g., neuromuscular demands) [7,8].
75	                     There are reports of German weightlifters using linear transducers in the 1970s [9]. Since
76	                     that time, research on the benefits of lifting velocity to prescribe and monitor RT has
77	                     been conducted [8,10–12]. Being able to objectively monitor RT sessions, adapt the goals
78	                     individually, or provide feedback in real time on a daily basis is paramount, especially when
79	                     working with elite players. In addition, compiling information will allow a critical analysis
80	                     based on objective data on the implemented methodology, and thus enable the necessary
81	                     adjustments and advancements in the knowledge of the strength training theory. However,
82	                     there are still some confusion, misinterpretations and wrong practices when implementing
83	                     VBT in team sports. Therefore, the aim of this article is to provide a comprehensive
84	                     overview of the main benefits, technologies and best practices when implementing VBT
85	                     programs in team sports.
86	
87	                     2. The Challenges and Drawbacks of the 1-Repetition Maximum Paradigm
88	                          The value of 1RM represents the maximal load (mass) that the athlete can lift, in a
89	                     concentric dynamic action, with proper form, once but not twice [13]. Thus, performing
90	                     a 1RM is considered a maximal dynamic effort. Once this value is known, programming
91	                     of RT is done prescribing relative loads to the individual’s 1RM [14,15]. However, this
92	                     methodology comes with certain disadvantages.
93	                          It is well known in the powerlifting community that experienced lifters are able
94	                     to move their 1RM load (mass) at a lower speed than their less trained or experienced
95	                     counterparts, especially in complex multi-joint exercises. Either due to inexperience, not
96	                     making a truly maximum effort or having experience but avoiding situations of risk of
97	                     injury using maximum loads, the 1RM is often poorly measured, which implies that the
98	                     consequent prescribed load (percentage-based training; nRM%), or velocities for each
99	                     1RM%, will not be adequate.
100	                          Moreover, as happens with other measures of physical performance, the 1RM could
101	                     vary on a daily basis due to several uncontrolled factors (e.g., fatigue, mental preparation,
102	                     sleep, stress or nutrition) [16]. Hence, in order to prescribe a precise load for each session,
103	                     the 1RM should be tested at the beginning of every RT session to adjust loads to the actual
104	                     (current) daily maximal capabilities of the athlete. However, since conducting an actual
105	                     1RM test before each training session is utopic, traditional percentage-based approaches
106	                     have been used, where the 1RM is assessed at the beginning of a training cycle, the %RM is
107	                     calculated and the RT program periodized for the subsequent weeks according to it [12,17].
108	                     The main drawback with this approach is that, since the actual 1RM could vary from
109	                     one session to another, the subsequent prescribed loads (mass) for the cycle would likely
110	                     represent a different effort to the initial loads (%RM) programed based on the original 1RM.
111	                     As an illustration of this potential discrepancy, Table 1 displays a RT load progression over
112	                     a period of 8-weeks, with one example based on the 1RM assessed prior to the training
113	                     cycle, and an example based on daily estimations using load–velocity profiles.
114	                          Additionally, the effort that represents each 1RM percentage differs between exer-
115	                     cises [18,19], where, for example, the 85% 1RM represents a different effort in bench press
116	                     vs. back squat. Furthermore, the load that represents a %1RM still requires performing
117	                     repetitions to failure, and extensive research has shown that performing repetitions to mus-
118	                     cular failure can impair performance, at specific times of a periodization program, due to an
119	                     excessive production of fatigue, thus making it inappropriate for team sports training [20].
120	 Sports 2021, 9, 47                                                                                                                                  3 of 14
121	
122	
123	
124	      Table 1. Comparison of the load associated with 70% 1-Repetition Maximum (1RM), using the pre-test value (session 1) or
125	      actual daily values.
126	
127	                            Session 1        Session 2       Session 3       Session 4       Session 5       Session 6       Session 7        Session 8
128	      1RM (kg)                  130              —               —               —               —                —               —               —
129	   Load @ 70%1RM

131	        (kg)
132	  Actual daily 1RM              130            132.5            130              135            137.5           132.5            135             140

135	        (kg)

137	      were used as a reference in the “pretest programming”, while daily 1RM scores estimated by measuring barbell velocity were used in the
138	      “daily programming”. Note that in the pre-test programming, every session would have been performed with 91 kg (i.e., the 70% of the
139	      pre-test 1RM), but if daily variations would have been taken into account, the actual load would have variated on a daily basis.
140	
141	
142	                                      3. Technologies to Track Velocity for Resistance Training
143	                                            Due to the growing interest in VBT, there has been a proliferation of devices measuring
144	                                      velocity for RT, from motion capture systems (MoCap), linear transducers and accelerome-
145	                                      ters, to low-cost smartphone apps. In addition, this phenomenon has been accompanied
146	                                      by a number of studies conducted on the validity and reliability of some of these novel
147	                                      technologies to measure velocity [21–29]. However, each of these technologies has advan-
148	                                      tages and disadvantages, and practitioners tasked with managing the systems have the
149	                                      responsibility to understand the pros and cons of the different systems, as well as using a
150	                                      systematic process in the data collection, being knowledgeable on best practices regarding
151	                                      implementing VBT, and applying critical thinking when assessing their RT methodologies.
152	                                            Team sports rarely require static, linear or single-joint movements. Rather, it is the
153	                                      opposite in that there are not only complex movements but also ones performed in highly
154	                                      unpredictable environments and with opponents (involving contact, perturbations, colli-
155	                                      sions, and such). Velocity tracking systems are still far from being able to measure with
156	                                      ecological validity; most are designed to measure traditional strength exercises, connected
157	                                      to equipment, or to certain body segments.
158	                                            Linear transducers are probably one of the most popular technologies used in the
159	                                      implementation of VBT to date. One of the downsides is that they are limited to measure
160	                                      vertical motion only [30,31]. Most commercial models available in the market just measure
161	                                      the vertical component of the velocity vector, meaning that any horizontal or lateral motion
162	                                      during the lift would be (and should be) omitted (Figure 1). Horizontal displacements
163	                                      do occur when using free weights even in “vertical” exercises like the back squat [32,33];
164	                                      hence, a proper exercise form and technique should be guaranteed, and exercises with a
165	                                      horizontal or angular momentum component avoided.
166	                                            In most cases, linear transducers are attached to one end of a barbell, and thus they
167	                                      actually register the velocity of that part of the bar, which could differ from the velocity
168	                                      of the other end if the athlete did not lift it perfectly, parallel to the ground. Lifting an
169	                                      unbalanced barbell does happen in practice, and S&C coaches using linear transducers
170	                                      should be aware of this fact. To reduce this type of error in the measurement, some studies
171	                                      have used two linear transducers, and reported the mean velocity registered from the two
172	                                      devices [30,32]. This may not be feasible in applied contexts; an alternative support may
173	                                      be having a visual control of the form of execution (objective or subjective) and exclude
174	                                      incorrect repetitions. It is then recommended that the device is placed consistently on the
175	                                      same side.
176	                                            Trying to solve some of the aforementioned limitations, different novel technologies
177	                                      such as accelerometers or smartphone apps have emerged as a cost-effective and prac-
178	                                      tical alternative to measure movement velocity in resistance exercises, and studies have
179	                                      shown that they can do it in a valid and reliable way [22,25,28,34]. For example, certain
180	                                      accelerometers can track velocity in exercises with horizontal displacement, while apps
181	                                      have shown reliable measurement of mean concentric velocity in cable-based exercises
182	 Sports 2021, 9, 47                                                                                                   4 of 14
183	
184	
185	
186	                     by video-recording the vertical ascent of the machine’s weight stack [35]. However, these
187	                     devices come with their own limitations. While they have shown moderate to good validity
188	                     and reliability, accelerometers had the lowest accuracy when compared with other devices,
189	                     such as linear transducers, apps, MoCap or gold-standard instruments [22,28]. A popular
190	                     app [25] has presented validity, reliability and accuracy higher than accelerometers; how-
191	                     ever, since it is video-based (frame-to-frame slow motion navigation), the measurements
192	                     are not provided in real time. When comparing different linear transducers, studies have
193	                     observed differences in absolute velocity outputs [28]. Thus, when interpreting VBT re-
194	                     search (especially when looking to raw velocity data) practitioners should interpret results
195	                     carefully; it is advised to not use devices from different manufactures interchangeably.
196	
197	
198	
199	
200	                     Figure 1. Generic linear transducer showing a deviation of 20◦ from the vertical during a lift.
201	                     For a registered mean velocity of 0.82 m·s−1 , the actual magnitude of the resultant mean velocity
202	                     vector would be 0.87 m/s, as calculated using simple trigonometry (Actual velocity = Registered
203	                     velocity/cos (angle). Most of the load–velocity relationships analyzed in the scientific literature are
204	                     conducted with exercises performed in Smith machines, since this equipment guarantees a complete
205	                     vertical motion of the barbell. This, however, reduces the ecological validity of the load–velocity
206	                     relationship itself, since these profiles can differ if the lift is performed with free weights (where
207	                     horizontal displacements occur) or with a Smith machine.
208	
209	                           Another common misappropriation of technologies to track movement velocity is
210	                     its application for the measurement of power or “muscle power”. Power is important in
211	                     sport because it is an expression of performance, the consequence of the force applied in a
212	                     given time in a given action, which is paramount in many sport activities [36–38]. It is a
213	                     product of force and velocity, but depending on how force and velocity are calculated, the
214	                     resultant “power output” can vary [30,36]. How force is calculated has a great impact on
215	 Sports 2021, 9, 47                                                                                           5 of 14
216	
217	
218	
219	                     the “power output”, producing contradictory findings that can confuse S&C coaches. For
220	                     example, studies that have analyzed the load that maximizes power output in different
221	                     exercises have found heterogenous results, with wide observed ranges (from 30 to 80%
222	                     1RM) that still make it challenging to come to a consensus about which load elicits the
223	                     maximal power output [30,39–42]. Likely, the main reason for those discrepancies is the
224	                     method used to calculate the force. The gold standard to measure force production in
225	                     dynamic actions, such as jumping or lifting, are force plates [30,43]; they are designed to
226	                     continuously measure force exerted on them, and calculate the force applied to the system
227	                     mass (e.g., the bodyweight of the athlete plus the mass of the barbell), when performing the
228	                     exercise. Most velocity tracking systems (e.g., linear transducers, accelerometers, MoCap)
229	                     do not take into account the athlete’s bodyweight (mass) in their “power” calculations;
230	                     therefore, reviewing whether they are included in the force calculation is advised). Instead,
231	                     they calculate it by the differentiation in the velocity measured to obtain acceleration, and
232	                     afterward multiply it to the mass of the barbell [41,43]. This method has been proven to
233	                     underestimate the actual power (force applied at a given velocity), when pushing to the
234	                     ground when jumping [44]. Studies using “barbell power” measurement have observed
235	                     that the load that maximizes power in vertical jumps, or ballistic bench press throws, are
236	                     much higher than those using the “system power” [36,41,45,46]. For example, if the body
237	                     mass (aka system mass) is considered in the calculation of force, the load that maximizes
238	                     power output is close to 0 kg (i.e., unloaded jump), while, when considering only the
239	                     barbell mass, the load that maximizes power output is close to 100% of body weight for
240	                     the external load [46]. Thus, the practical recommendation to maximize “power output”
241	                     during vertical jumping can be completely different if the system mass or the barbell mass
242	                     is used in the calculation of force. Although “barbell power output” could be of great
243	                     interest for athletes whose main activity is to apply maximum power to an implement
244	                     (e.g., throwing), it is our opinion that it is not the most appropriate method when assessing
245	                     power production capabilities in team sport players. Nonetheless, if the goal the S&C
246	                     coach is to measure “power output”, they are encouraged to use force platforms and
247	                     include the total mass (athlete body mass and external mass) in the computations from the
248	                     linear transducer.
249	                           Finally, it is worth noting that different manufacturers might report different velocity
250	                     metrics, with the most popular being MVC, mean concentric velocity of the propulsive
251	                     phase (MPV) and/or peak velocity (PV) [8,29,47]. While it has been proposed that MPV can
252	                     better represent the velocity production ability of the athlete [48], it has also been observed
253	                     that mean concentric velocity (MCV)is as reliable as MPV [47], and, from a technological
254	                     point of view, simpler to measure. It is also worth mentioning that, considering that MCV,
255	                     MPV and PV are different (generally, MCV < MPV < PV), these metrics should not be used
256	                     interchangeably. For standardization purposes, in this document we refer to MCV when
257	                     citing velocity of execution.
258	
259	                     4. Determination of Individual Load–Velocity Profiles in Team Sport
260	                          Early technology used to measure velocity was expensive, not accessible to the vast
261	                     majority of practitioners and mainly constrained to measure vertical motions (e.g., linear
262	                     transducers). Nowadays, there are more accessible devices, capable of measuring the
263	                     velocity in different types of equipment, which allow the assessment of numerous exercises
264	                     simultaneously (e.g., a player being able to track a session in multiple exercises or players
265	                     working at the same time in different stations). The latest point, working with large squads,
266	                     is probably one of the biggest challenges when it comes to measuring (or testing) in team
267	                     sports, since time can be a constraint. Velocity tracking systems are evolving, making
268	                     assessment procedures less time consuming for both coaches and players. However, there
269	                     are some key aspects to take into account to successfully implement VBT during the RT
270	                     session with team sport athletes.
271	                          The vast majority of the exercises analyzed in the VBT literature arebarbell-
272	                     based [8,49–51], and researchers have found an almost a perfect association between
273	 Sports 2021, 9, 47                                                                                                6 of 14
274	
275	
276	
277	                     mean concentric velocity (MCV) and load (%1RM) in several exercises, such as bench-
278	                     press, back squat, deadlift or hip-thrust. Some studies have also observed that the load–
279	                     velocity relationship is well-fitted in machine and cable-based exercises (e.g., the leg
280	                     extension) [35]. What is important to highlight here is that the load–velocity relationship
281	                     is exercise-dependent [18,52,53], since the load that represents a certain absolute velocity
282	                     can vary greatly between exercises (Table 2). Thus, the use of absolute “velocity zones”
283	                     is discouraged, since a certain velocity (e.g., 1.0 m·s−1 ) can represent a low load (mass)
284	                     (e.g., when performing a back squat) or a near maximal load (e.g., when performing an
285	                     Olympic Snatch). Including a battery of one lower-body, one upper-body, and/or full body
286	                     multi-joint barbell exercises in the assessment is recommended.
287	
288	                     Table 2. Velocities for different %1RM from an individual load–velocity profile of one player, for
289	                     bench-press, back squat, deadlift and pull-up exercises [8,18,52,53].

313	                           The load–velocity profile is created by calculating a regression that fits the veloc-
314	                     ity (data points) with different loads (absolute or relative), where the more loads as-
315	                     sessed, the higher the accuracy of the profile. However, including a high number of loads
316	                     (e.g., 10 loads) would be time consuming and impractical when testing a large squad of
317	                     players. Moreover, in order to avoid fatigue and guarantee that the athletes are performing
318	                     the lift at their maximal velocity capabilities, a passive rest of 3 to 5 min between loads is
319	                     needed. Consequently, it is recommended to select a number of loads (mass; data points)
320	                     that is time efficient but, at the same time, that guarantees a regression fit. It was observed
321	                     that profiles created from two loads can be as reliable as those created from six loads, as
322	                     long as the loads used are properly selected; in this case, it seems that a light load (about
323	                     40% 1RM) and a heavy load (about 80% 1RM) are the best options [11,54]. However, if
324	                     one of the two loads are not properly performed (i.e., athletes not applying their maxi-
325	                     mal intended velocity), the results can be drastically altered. Therefore, we recommend
326	                     performing between 4 and 6 sets with incremental loads to guarantee that the results are
327	                     reliable (Table 3).
328	                           Research has shown that subjective scales are highly related with MCV in different
329	                     resistance exercises [55–57]. For example, it has been observed that both the Repetitions in
330	                     Reserve (RIR) (calculated as the number or % of repetitions performed with respect to the
331	                     maximum number of possible repetitions) and the Rating of Perceived Exertion (RPE) scores
332	                     are associated with velocity loss with different loads [58]. Hence, accounting for the RIR
333	                     and/or RPE can be useful tools when programming, and for understanding the mechanical
334	                     fatigue that the athlete is experiencing without having to measure the velocity drop over the
335	 Sports 2021, 9, 47                                                                                                                   7 of 14
336	
337	
338	
339	                     set. Moreover, it has been shown that the inclusion of RIR with the movement velocity in a
340	                     multiple regression improves the accuracy of the load–velocity profile [59]. While practitioners
341	                     should ideally measure MCV in most of the main exercises, prescribing RT using RIR can
342	                     be a suitable solution in those exercises where calculating the load–velocity profiles might
343	                     be of less interest or not suitable, such as dumbbell, cable, kettlebell exercises, and the like.
344	                     Moreover, it has been observed in youth basketball players that training using a RIR approach
345	                     is more suitable than conducting traditional repetitions to failure when velocity is not used to
346	                     monitor training load [60]. Table 4 presents a VBT training prescription where some exercises
347	                     are prescribed using velocity, and others are based on RIR.

                     prescribe RT based on velocity of execution. This is a key element in most sport disciplines,
                     either by the requirements of the sport (e.g., sprinting, accelerating/decelerating, jumping,
                     throwing, kicking) or as an indicator of intensity (e.g., neuromuscular demands) [7,8].
                     There are reports of German weightlifters using linear transducers in the 1970s [9]. Since
                     that time, research on the benefits of lifting velocity to prescribe and monitor RT has
                     been conducted [8,10–12]. Being able to objectively monitor RT sessions, adapt the goals
                     individually, or provide feedback in real time on a daily basis is paramount, especially when
                     working with elite players. In addition, compiling information will allow a critical analysis
                     based on objective data on the implemented methodology, and thus enable the necessary
                     adjustments and advancements in the knowledge of the strength training theory. However,
                     there are still some confusion, misinterpretations and wrong practices when implementing
                     VBT in team sports. Therefore, the aim of this article is to provide a comprehensive
                     overview of the main benefits, technologies and best practices when implementing VBT
                     programs in team sports.

                     2. The Challenges and Drawbacks of the 1-Repetition Maximum Paradigm
                          The value of 1RM represents the maximal load (mass) that the athlete can lift, in a
                     concentric dynamic action, with proper form, once but not twice [13]. Thus, performing
                     a 1RM is considered a maximal dynamic effort. Once this value is known, programming
                     of RT is done prescribing relative loads to the individual’s 1RM [14,15]. However, this
                     methodology comes with certain disadvantages.
                          It is well known in the powerlifting community that experienced lifters are able
                     to move their 1RM load (mass) at a lower speed than their less trained or experienced
                     counterparts, especially in complex multi-joint exercises. Either due to inexperience, not
                     making a truly maximum effort or having experience but avoiding situations of risk of
                     injury using maximum loads, the 1RM is often poorly measured, which implies that the
                     consequent prescribed load (percentage-based training; nRM%), or velocities for each
                     1RM%, will not be adequate.
                          Moreover, as happens with other measures of physical performance, the 1RM could
                     vary on a daily basis due to several uncontrolled factors (e.g., fatigue, mental preparation,
                     sleep, stress or nutrition) [16]. Hence, in order to prescribe a precise load for each session,
                     the 1RM should be tested at the beginning of every RT session to adjust loads to the actual
                     (current) daily maximal capabilities of the athlete. However, since conducting an actual
                     1RM test before each training session is utopic, traditional percentage-based approaches
                     have been used, where the 1RM is assessed at the beginning of a training cycle, the %RM is
                     calculated and the RT program periodized for the subsequent weeks according to it [12,17].
                     The main drawback with this approach is that, since the actual 1RM could vary from
                     one session to another, the subsequent prescribed loads (mass) for the cycle would likely
                     represent a different effort to the initial loads (%RM) programed based on the original 1RM.
                     As an illustration of this potential discrepancy, Table 1 displays a RT load progression over
                     a period of 8-weeks, with one example based on the 1RM assessed prior to the training
                     cycle, and an example based on daily estimations using load–velocity profiles.
                          Additionally, the effort that represents each 1RM percentage differs between exer-
                     cises [18,19], where, for example, the 85% 1RM represents a different effort in bench press
                     vs. back squat. Furthermore, the load that represents a %1RM still requires performing
                     repetitions to failure, and extensive research has shown that performing repetitions to mus-
                     cular failure can impair performance, at specific times of a periodization program, due to an
                     excessive production of fatigue, thus making it inappropriate for team sports training [20].

                                      3. Technologies to Track Velocity for Resistance Training
                                            Due to the growing interest in VBT, there has been a proliferation of devices measuring
                                      velocity for RT, from motion capture systems (MoCap), linear transducers and accelerome-
                                      ters, to low-cost smartphone apps. In addition, this phenomenon has been accompanied
                                      by a number of studies conducted on the validity and reliability of some of these novel
                                      technologies to measure velocity [21–29]. However, each of these technologies has advan-
                                      tages and disadvantages, and practitioners tasked with managing the systems have the
                                      responsibility to understand the pros and cons of the different systems, as well as using a
                                      systematic process in the data collection, being knowledgeable on best practices regarding
                                      implementing VBT, and applying critical thinking when assessing their RT methodologies.
                                            Team sports rarely require static, linear or single-joint movements. Rather, it is the
                                      opposite in that there are not only complex movements but also ones performed in highly
                                      unpredictable environments and with opponents (involving contact, perturbations, colli-
                                      sions, and such). Velocity tracking systems are still far from being able to measure with
                                      ecological validity; most are designed to measure traditional strength exercises, connected
                                      to equipment, or to certain body segments.
                                            Linear transducers are probably one of the most popular technologies used in the
                                      implementation of VBT to date. One of the downsides is that they are limited to measure
                                      vertical motion only [30,31]. Most commercial models available in the market just measure
                                      the vertical component of the velocity vector, meaning that any horizontal or lateral motion
                                      during the lift would be (and should be) omitted (Figure 1). Horizontal displacements
                                      do occur when using free weights even in “vertical” exercises like the back squat [32,33];
                                      hence, a proper exercise form and technique should be guaranteed, and exercises with a
                                      horizontal or angular momentum component avoided.
                                            In most cases, linear transducers are attached to one end of a barbell, and thus they
                                      actually register the velocity of that part of the bar, which could differ from the velocity
                                      of the other end if the athlete did not lift it perfectly, parallel to the ground. Lifting an
                                      unbalanced barbell does happen in practice, and S&C coaches using linear transducers
                                      should be aware of this fact. To reduce this type of error in the measurement, some studies
                                      have used two linear transducers, and reported the mean velocity registered from the two
                                      devices [30,32]. This may not be feasible in applied contexts; an alternative support may
                                      be having a visual control of the form of execution (objective or subjective) and exclude
                                      incorrect repetitions. It is then recommended that the device is placed consistently on the
                                      same side.
                                            Trying to solve some of the aforementioned limitations, different novel technologies
                                      such as accelerometers or smartphone apps have emerged as a cost-effective and prac-
                                      tical alternative to measure movement velocity in resistance exercises, and studies have
                                      shown that they can do it in a valid and reliable way [22,25,28,34]. For example, certain
                                      accelerometers can track velocity in exercises with horizontal displacement, while apps
                                      have shown reliable measurement of mean concentric velocity in cable-based exercises
 Sports 2021, 9, 47                                                                                                   4 of 14



                     by video-recording the vertical ascent of the machine’s weight stack [35]. However, these
                     devices come with their own limitations. While they have shown moderate to good validity
                     and reliability, accelerometers had the lowest accuracy when compared with other devices,
                     such as linear transducers, apps, MoCap or gold-standard instruments [22,28]. A popular
                     app [25] has presented validity, reliability and accuracy higher than accelerometers; how-
                     ever, since it is video-based (frame-to-frame slow motion navigation), the measurements
                     are not provided in real time. When comparing different linear transducers, studies have
                     observed differences in absolute velocity outputs [28]. Thus, when interpreting VBT re-
                     search (especially when looking to raw velocity data) practitioners should interpret results
                     carefully; it is advised to not use devices from different manufactures interchangeably.




                     Figure 1. Generic linear transducer showing a deviation of 20◦ from the vertical during a lift.
                     For a registered mean velocity of 0.82 m·s−1 , the actual magnitude of the resultant mean velocity
                     vector would be 0.87 m/s, as calculated using simple trigonometry (Actual velocity = Registered
                     velocity/cos (angle). Most of the load–velocity relationships analyzed in the scientific literature are
                     conducted with exercises performed in Smith machines, since this equipment guarantees a complete
                     vertical motion of the barbell. This, however, reduces the ecological validity of the load–velocity
                     relationship itself, since these profiles can differ if the lift is performed with free weights (where
                     horizontal displacements occur) or with a Smith machine.

                           Another common misappropriation of technologies to track movement velocity is
                     its application for the measurement of power or “muscle power”. Power is important in
                     sport because it is an expression of performance, the consequence of the force applied in a
                     given time in a given action, which is paramount in many sport activities [36–38]. It is a
                     product of force and velocity, but depending on how force and velocity are calculated, the
                     resultant “power output” can vary [30,36]. How force is calculated has a great impact on
 Sports 2021, 9, 47                                                                                           5 of 14



                     the “power output”, producing contradictory findings that can confuse S&C coaches. For
                     example, studies that have analyzed the load that maximizes power output in different
                     exercises have found heterogenous results, with wide observed ranges (from 30 to 80%
                     1RM) that still make it challenging to come to a consensus about which load elicits the
                     maximal power output [30,39–42]. Likely, the main reason for those discrepancies is the
                     method used to calculate the force. The gold standard to measure force production in
                     dynamic actions, such as jumping or lifting, are force plates [30,43]; they are designed to
                     continuously measure force exerted on them, and calculate the force applied to the system
                     mass (e.g., the bodyweight of the athlete plus the mass of the barbell), when performing the
                     exercise. Most velocity tracking systems (e.g., linear transducers, accelerometers, MoCap)
                     do not take into account the athlete’s bodyweight (mass) in their “power” calculations;
                     therefore, reviewing whether they are included in the force calculation is advised). Instead,
                     they calculate it by the differentiation in the velocity measured to obtain acceleration, and
                     afterward multiply it to the mass of the barbell [41,43]. This method has been proven to
                     underestimate the actual power (force applied at a given velocity), when pushing to the
                     ground when jumping [44]. Studies using “barbell power” measurement have observed
                     that the load that maximizes power in vertical jumps, or ballistic bench press throws, are
                     much higher than those using the “system power” [36,41,45,46]. For example, if the body
                     mass (aka system mass) is considered in the calculation of force, the load that maximizes
                     power output is close to 0 kg (i.e., unloaded jump), while, when considering only the
                     barbell mass, the load that maximizes power output is close to 100% of body weight for
                     the external load [46]. Thus, the practical recommendation to maximize “power output”
                     during vertical jumping can be completely different if the system mass or the barbell mass
                     is used in the calculation of force. Although “barbell power output” could be of great
                     interest for athletes whose main activity is to apply maximum power to an implement
                     (e.g., throwing), it is our opinion that it is not the most appropriate method when assessing
                     power production capabilities in team sport players. Nonetheless, if the goal the S&C
                     coach is to measure “power output”, they are encouraged to use force platforms and
                     include the total mass (athlete body mass and external mass) in the computations from the
                     linear transducer.
                           Finally, it is worth noting that different manufacturers might report different velocity
                     metrics, with the most popular being MVC, mean concentric velocity of the propulsive
                     phase (MPV) and/or peak velocity (PV) [8,29,47]. While it has been proposed that MPV can
                     better represent the velocity production ability of the athlete [48], it has also been observed
                     that mean concentric velocity (MCV)is as reliable as MPV [47], and, from a technological
                     point of view, simpler to measure. It is also worth mentioning that, considering that MCV,
                     MPV and PV are different (generally, MCV < MPV < PV), these metrics should not be used
                     interchangeably. For standardization purposes, in this document we refer to MCV when
                     citing velocity of execution.

                     4. Determination of Individual Load–Velocity Profiles in Team Sport
                          Early technology used to measure velocity was expensive, not accessible to the vast
                     majority of practitioners and mainly constrained to measure vertical motions (e.g., linear
                     transducers). Nowadays, there are more accessible devices, capable of measuring the
                     velocity in different types of equipment, which allow the assessment of numerous exercises
                     simultaneously (e.g., a player being able to track a session in multiple exercises or players
                     working at the same time in different stations). The latest point, working with large squads,
                     is probably one of the biggest challenges when it comes to measuring (or testing) in team
                     sports, since time can be a constraint. Velocity tracking systems are evolving, making
                     assessment procedures less time consuming for both coaches and players. However, there
                     are some key aspects to take into account to successfully implement VBT during the RT
                     session with team sport athletes.
                          The vast majority of the exercises analyzed in the VBT literature arebarbell-
                     based [8,49–51], and researchers have found an almost a perfect association between
 Sports 2021, 9, 47                                                                                                6 of 14



                     mean concentric velocity (MCV) and load (%1RM) in several exercises, such as bench-
                     press, back squat, deadlift or hip-thrust. Some studies have also observed that the load–
                     velocity relationship is well-fitted in machine and cable-based exercises (e.g., the leg
                     extension) [35]. What is important to highlight here is that the load–velocity relationship
                     is exercise-dependent [18,52,53], since the load that represents a certain absolute velocity
                     can vary greatly between exercises (Table 2). Thus, the use of absolute “velocity zones”
                     is discouraged, since a certain velocity (e.g., 1.0 m·s−1 ) can represent a low load (mass)
                     (e.g., when performing a back squat) or a near maximal load (e.g., when performing an
                     Olympic Snatch). Including a battery of one lower-body, one upper-body, and/or full body
                     multi-joint barbell exercises in the assessment is recommended.

                           The load–velocity profile is created by calculating a regression that fits the veloc-
                     ity (data points) with different loads (absolute or relative), where the more loads as-
                     sessed, the higher the accuracy of the profile. However, including a high number of loads
                     (e.g., 10 loads) would be time consuming and impractical when testing a large squad of
                     players. Moreover, in order to avoid fatigue and guarantee that the athletes are performing
                     the lift at their maximal velocity capabilities, a passive rest of 3 to 5 min between loads is
                     needed. Consequently, it is recommended to select a number of loads (mass; data points)
                     that is time efficient but, at the same time, that guarantees a regression fit. It was observed
                     that profiles created from two loads can be as reliable as those created from six loads, as
                     long as the loads used are properly selected; in this case, it seems that a light load (about
                     40% 1RM) and a heavy load (about 80% 1RM) are the best options [11,54]. However, if
                     one of the two loads are not properly performed (i.e., athletes not applying their maxi-
                     mal intended velocity), the results can be drastically altered. Therefore, we recommend
                     performing between 4 and 6 sets with incremental loads to guarantee that the results are
                     reliable (Table 3).
                           Research has shown that subjective scales are highly related with MCV in different
                     resistance exercises [55–57]. For example, it has been observed that both the Repetitions in
                     Reserve (RIR) (calculated as the number or % of repetitions performed with respect to the
                     maximum number of possible repetitions) and the Rating of Perceived Exertion (RPE) scores
                     are associated with velocity loss with different loads [58]. Hence, accounting for the RIR
                     and/or RPE can be useful tools when programming, and for understanding the mechanical
                     fatigue that the athlete is experiencing without having to measure the velocity drop over the

                     set. Moreover, it has been shown that the inclusion of RIR with the movement velocity in a
                     multiple regression improves the accuracy of the load–velocity profile [59]. While practitioners
                     should ideally measure MCV in most of the main exercises, prescribing RT using RIR can
                     be a suitable solution in those exercises where calculating the load–velocity profiles might
                     be of less interest or not suitable, such as dumbbell, cable, kettlebell exercises, and the like.
                     Moreover, it has been observed in youth basketball players that training using a RIR approach
                     is more suitable than conducting traditional repetitions to failure when velocity is not used to
                     monitor training load [60]. Table 4 presents a VBT training prescription where some exercises

                     5. Considerations for a Successful Implementation of a Velocity-Based Program
                          The velocity of execution (during the concentric phase of dynamic exercises) is a key
                     training variable in sports performance. In the following, we present some important
                     remarks when implementing VBT:
                     •    The most relevant consideration when training based on the velocity of execution
                          (VBT) is that velocity must be the maximal intended. If the athlete does not perform
                          with a maximal intended velocity (regardless of the load (mass) or %1RM), the results
                          would be underestimated [61].

                          ogy based on the velocity of execution, used to prescribe, monitor and analyze RT.
                          The velocity of execution can be used at different %RM (percentage-based training),
                          including heavy loads; choosing appropriate and key exercises is paramount.

                          individual load–velocity profiles are computed is very stable [62]. Therefore, the
                          velocity of execution with a fixed absolute load can be a good indicator of effort and
                          actual (current) performance.

                          1RM (Table 2).

422	                     •    Practitioners can benefit from combining objective and subjective scales to improve the
423	                          accuracy of the training load prescription. As observed in a recent review on the topic,
424	                          both objective (i.e., mean concentric velocity) and subjective measurements (i.e., repe-
425	                          titions in reserve) can help to enhance muscular strength by prescribing training loads
426	                          that take into account the athlete’s daily fluctuations in performance or fatigue [66].
427	                          Moreover, it has been observed that the combination of MCV and RIR increases the
428	                          accuracy of the 1RM estimation in comparison with using MCV alone [59].
429	                     •    The mean velocity might represent different levels of effort depending on the an-
430	                          thropometric profile. It is paramount to create individual load–velocity profiles for
431	                          each athlete, especially if the players within a team have large differences in their
432	                          anthropometrics. This can be especially relevant in sports like basketball, where limb
433	                          lengths can have a wide range between players. For example, two players can lift the
434	                          same relative load (i.e., %1RM) in the bench press at 0.8 m·s−1 , but player-A barbell’s
435	                          displacement is 0.35 m, while for player-B it is 0.6 m; this means that player-B has pro-
436	                          duced the same velocity as player-A, but in almost twice the time (0.75 s for player-B
437	                          vs. 0.43 s for player-A). Thus, player-B spends more time under tension, meaning that
438	                          the overall effort for the same velocity might be higher for player-B than for player-A.
439	
440	                     6. Prescribing and Monitoring Training Loads with VBT
441	                          There are certain methodological aspects when using velocity of execution during
442	                     RT that can be relevant as indicators of effort and for monitoring training on a daily basis.
443	                     As a starting point, practitioners could choose key exercises for the training cycle, and
444	                     determine a load–velocity profile for those. Secondly, the relative intensities of the training
445	                     cycle (e.g., %RM) should be defined. Thereafter, measure the velocity in the first set of an
446	                     exercises to establish subsequent loads for the day; to do that on a daily basis, practitioners
447	                     would choose a fixed load (mass) for the warm-up, perform one set of 1–2 repetitions and
448	                     measure the MCV. Once the velocity at the fixed load is known for that day/exercise, adjust
449	                     loads to the actual (current) daily maximal capabilities of the athlete that represents the
450	                     intended velocity for the programmed intensity (%RM). Figure 2 displays an example of a
451	                     player’s load–velocity profile, the speed for the warm-up repetition, and the corresponding
452	                     %RM. The faster the velocity, the lower the percentage of the 1RM that the load represents.
453	 Sports 2021, 9, 47                                                                                                                 9 of 14
454	
455	
456	
457	
458	      Figure 2. Estimation of daily 1RM scores on the back squat using individual load–velocity profile of the player. In this
459	      example, if the athlete has lifted the 90 kg at 0.49 m·s−1 ; according to his individual profile, that represents his 85% 1RM.
460	      Consequently, the theoretical 1RM of that day would be 105.6 kg.
461	
462	                                         Finally, prescribe the number of repetitions per set by either: (i) the velocity loss
463	                                  thresholds within the series, (ii) the repetitions in reserve, or (iii) using subjective scales. A
464	                                  relevant use of VBT when prescribing RT sessions is being able to identify neuromuscular
465	                                  fatigue and modify the number repetitions the athlete should perform during the set [10,67].
466	                                  It has been observed that velocity loss during the set is highly related with markers of
467	                                  fatigue such as lactate or ammonia [68]. Studies have observed that low velocity loss
468	                                  thresholds (i.e., 10–20% loss from the fastest repetition) can produce similar improvements
469	                                  in physical performance with significantly lower training volume than higher thresholds
470	                                  (i.e., 40% loss or more) [67,69] On the contrary, if the RT goal is to maximize muscle mass,
471	                                  research has shown that lifting close to muscular failure is more adequate [70,71], and it
472	                                  has been observed that high velocity loss thresholds (i.e., 40% or more, which means going
473	                                  closer to failure) would be more appropriate to increase hypertrophy [69].
474	                                         The goal of strength training in sport is to improve force, velocity and power output
475	                                  production capabilities [37]. A positive training program would change MCV with a fixed
476	                                  absolute load/s or the load that can be lifted at a fixed speed. It has been shown that load–
477	                                  velocity profiles (i.e., the velocity associated with each %1RM) can be altered after a period
478	                                  of training of 4 to 6 weeks [49,72]. Thus, it is recommended to re-assess the load–velocity
479	                                  profile every ≈4–6 weeks, or after specific cycles of RT, in order to evaluate the effects of
480	                                  the RT. However, the training capacity of the athlete might vary on a daily basis, and that
481	                                  is why the measurement of the velocity execution in the first series or repetitions of an
482	                                  exercise is useful for the programming of each training session. Some velocity tracking
483	                                  systems (e.g., My Lift App, Madrid, Spain) include calculations within their algorithms that
484	                                  estimate 1RM on a daily basis by measuring individual load–velocity profiles, as explained
485	                                  in Figure 2.
486	 Sports 2021, 9, 47                                                                                                             10 of 14
487	
488	
489	
490	                                        Finally, in order to analyze the evolution of the players, we propose to “put the I back
491	                                  in team”, as nicely discussed in Ward et al. [73]. A current limitation in the strength and
492	                                  RT research is that most results provide group averages. Yet, to better optimize players’
493	                                  performance, an individual analysis is paramount. In order to analyze individual trends,
494	                                  proper statistical techniques should be implemented. Ward et al., in their 2018 study,
495	                                  proposed different statistical strategies to analyze the evolution over time of a single athlete.
496	                                  Figure 3 provides an example of day-to-day variation in bench-press performance over
497	                                  8-weeks.
498	
499

503	      (calculated as the average score of the previous 2 months), while the dark green, green, yellow and red shadowed areas
504	      represent +1 standard deviations (SD), +0.9 to −0.9 SD, −1 SD and −1.5 SD with respect to the baseline, respectively. Note
505	      that when there is no data in the weeks before the start of the training program, this approach cannot be used until enough
506	      data is collected.
507	
508	                                  7. Conclusions
509	                                        This manuscript aimed to provide a guideline to better implement VBT in team sport
510	                                  settings. The ultimate goal of RT in team sports is to improve the force production applied
511	                                  at a certain load (mass), at a given velocity and/or during a certain time. The velocity of
512	                                  execution is a reliable indicator of effort for programming and monitoring training, as well
513	                                  as for managing fatigue, both on a daily basis and in long term periodization.
514	                                        The advance in tracking systems allows measurement of an athlete’s velocity of
515	                                  execution during RT sessions, in different exercises during the same session, for a more
516	                                  comprehensive monitoring of the program. However, managing large squads during every
517	                                  training session can be challenging; how to best use technology in an efficient way, and
518	                                  educate coaches and players in its use, would be paramount.
519	                                        One consideration when using VBT tracking systems is the lack of research in their
520	                                  use in different strength training modalities, such as eccentric-overload training, pneumatic
521	                                  resistance or iso-inertial devices, and elastic-based equipment, where a velocity–effort
522	                                  (e.g., load (mass), %RM) relationship might not be the primary RT training goal with
523	                                  these tools.
524	 Sports 2021, 9, 47                                                                                                                11 of 14
525	
526	
527	
528	                                        Programming using VBT does not automatically imply programming effectively.
529	                                  The prescription, control, monitoring and evaluation of a RT using VBT requires a clear
530	                                  understanding of certain physics concepts, as well as strength training methodology. The
531	                                  VBT implementation should not be seen as an accessory to traditional RT or as a purely
532	                                  motivational tool for providing real-time feedback (the latter, without a doubt, being a great
533	                                  tool). The use of velocity in RT is a training paradigm, where specific strength goals and
534	                                  adaptations can be achieved by properly programming and tracking velocity of execution.
535	                                  It also allows for an objective quantification of the resistance training loads. Implementing
536	                                  VBT to monitor players’ performance can support decision-making processes, particularly
537	                                  the making of informed decisions when programing RT, and improvements in knowledge
538	                                  of the strength training paradigm.

                                  research has shown that lifting close to muscular failure is more adequate [70,71], and it
                                  has been observed that high velocity loss thresholds (i.e., 40% or more, which means going
                                  closer to failure) would be more appropriate to increase hypertrophy [69].
                                         The goal of strength training in sport is to improve force, velocity and power output
                                  production capabilities [37]. A positive training program would change MCV with a fixed
                                  absolute load/s or the load that can be lifted at a fixed speed. It has been shown that load–
                                  velocity profiles (i.e., the velocity associated with each %1RM) can be altered after a period
                                  of training of 4 to 6 weeks [49,72]. Thus, it is recommended to re-assess the load–velocity
                                  profile every ≈4–6 weeks, or after specific cycles of RT, in order to evaluate the effects of
                                  the RT. However, the training capacity of the athlete might vary on a daily basis, and that
                                  is why the measurement of the velocity execution in the first series or repetitions of an
                                  exercise is useful for the programming of each training session. Some velocity tracking
                                  systems (e.g., My Lift App, Madrid, Spain) include calculations within their algorithms that
                                  estimate 1RM on a daily basis by measuring individual load–velocity profiles, as explained
                                  in Figure 2.

                                        Finally, in order to analyze the evolution of the players, we propose to “put the I back
                                  in team”, as nicely discussed in Ward et al. [73]. A current limitation in the strength and
                                  RT research is that most results provide group averages. Yet, to better optimize players’
                                  performance, an individual analysis is paramount. In order to analyze individual trends,
                                  proper statistical techniques should be implemented. Ward et al., in their 2018 study,
                                  proposed different statistical strategies to analyze the evolution over time of a single athlete.
                                  Figure 3 provides an example of day-to-day variation in bench-press performance over
                                  8-weeks.




      Figure 3. Variation of bench-press 1RM over a period of 8 weeks. The black dashed line represents the baseline score
      (calculated as the average score of the previous 2 months), while the dark green, green, yellow and red shadowed areas
      represent +1 standard deviations (SD), +0.9 to −0.9 SD, −1 SD and −1.5 SD with respect to the baseline, respectively. Note
      that when there is no data in the weeks before the start of the training program, this approach cannot be used until enough
      data is collected.

                                  7. Conclusions
                                        This manuscript aimed to provide a guideline to better implement VBT in team sport
                                  settings. The ultimate goal of RT in team sports is to improve the force production applied
                                  at a certain load (mass), at a given velocity and/or during a certain time. The velocity of
                                  execution is a reliable indicator of effort for programming and monitoring training, as well
                                  as for managing fatigue, both on a daily basis and in long term periodization.
                                        The advance in tracking systems allows measurement of an athlete’s velocity of
                                  execution during RT sessions, in different exercises during the same session, for a more
                                  comprehensive monitoring of the program. However, managing large squads during every
                                  training session can be challenging; how to best use technology in an efficient way, and
                                  educate coaches and players in its use, would be paramount.
                                        One consideration when using VBT tracking systems is the lack of research in their
                                  use in different strength training modalities, such as eccentric-overload training, pneumatic
                                  resistance or iso-inertial devices, and elastic-based equipment, where a velocity–effort
                                  (e.g., load (mass), %RM) relationship might not be the primary RT training goal with
                                  these tools.

                                        Programming using VBT does not automatically imply programming effectively.
                                  The prescription, control, monitoring and evaluation of a RT using VBT requires a clear
                                  understanding of certain physics concepts, as well as strength training methodology. The
                                  VBT implementation should not be seen as an accessory to traditional RT or as a purely
                                  motivational tool for providing real-time feedback (the latter, without a doubt, being a great
                                  tool). The use of velocity in RT is a training paradigm, where specific strength goals and
                                  adaptations can be achieved by properly programming and tracking velocity of execution.
                                  It also allows for an objective quantification of the resistance training loads. Implementing
                                  VBT to monitor players’ performance can support decision-making processes, particularly
                                  the making of informed decisions when programing RT, and improvements in knowledge
                                  of the strength training paradigm.
